I've been working this land for 35 years, my father before me. I know what Quzhou soil does in a dry spring and a wet August. My wife handles the books while I handle the fields, and my son sends money from the city — so I'm not desperate to maximize every jin, but I still need the harvest to be worth my back.

All 16.9 mu rotates wheat into maize. Same ground, two seasons. That's how we've always done it here on the plain.

**Wheat (winter):** I'll plant in late October, right after the Mid-Autumn period. I'll use the Jimai improved variety I've been buying from the county seed station — not traditional seed, not the most expensive hybrid, but a proven improved line. I know it holds up to late frost. I'll put down base fertilizer at planting — compound fertilizer plus urea — and topdress nitrogen at jointing in March. Four irrigations: bottom water before planting, winter freeze water in December, jointing in late March, heading in late April. Water costs money with the pump, but skipping jointing water kills yield. Two pesticide passes — herbicide in winter and fungicide plus aphid spray at heading. I'll plough after the maize harvest to bury the stubble.

**Maize (summer):** Right after wheat harvest in June, I'll rotary-till and direct-seed hybrid maize — Zhengdan 958 or Xianyu 335, whichever the county supply cooperative has in stock. Hybrid is the only choice now; my neighbors who still use improved seed fall behind. One base fertilizer application, one topdress at big-flare stage. Maize has July rains to count on, but I'll irrigate twice — once at seedling if it's dry, once at silking if needed. Herbicide right after planting, then one pest pass mid-season for armyworm.

I keep my inputs roughly what my father used, maybe a bit more nitrogen — I know I probably over-apply, but I'm not taking chances on yield when prices are this low per jin. My margins come from volume.
